messages.subject: Data set for bilateral symmetry
parts:
Hello,
My name is Hardeep and I am fairly new to Geomorph package. I am trying to run the bilateral symmetry command and it seems to take forever to calculate. It does not provide any error, however, it also doesn't provide results. I have tried to run it with even fewer permutations.

My data looks like the following,
where I have wings data (Left and right wing) for more than 3000 individuals of the same species from 4 different locations (HR). I also have 3 replicated coordinates for each individual represented as 1,2,3 in the replicate column.

I am interested in size asymmetry between individuals of the same species from different geographical locations, thereby I gave the following command after the necessary transformation of raw coordinates. 

bs <- bilat.symmetry(A = data.gpa, ind = ind, side = side,
                     replicate = replicate,
                     object.sym = F, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 02,
                     data = data.gdf)



I believe something is wrong with individuals and replicate column... if it is in proper format?

Thank you for your time 
Kind regards,
Hardeep

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Data set for bilateral symmetry
parts:
Dear Hardeep,

Foremost, bilat.symmetry is working.  But for the analysis you have, time must be an asset to have in order to expect results.

The bilat.symmetry function uses randomization of residuals in a permutation procedure (RRPP) to create distributions of linear model or ANOVA statistics.  This is an iterative, non-parametric procedure, which for large data sets can have quite a computational (computer memory) burden compared to a parametric approach (more on that below).  There are ways to speed up the analysis.  For example, the Parallel argument in the function can be changed to include parallel processing, if you have a computer with several processors and sufficient memory to handle that operation.

As a demonstration of what you are up against, based on the limited information you provided, a data set with 3000 individuals digitized 6 times each (three left and three right) would incur a linear model design matrix as such:

> ind <- factor(rep(1:3000, each = 6))
> side <- factor(rep(c(1,1,1, 2,2,2), 3000))
> X <- model.matrix(~ind * side)
> dim(X)
[1] 18000  6000
> object.size(X)
865585352 bytes

Just the 18,000 x 6,000 design matrix is 865 MB in size!  This is only one of several design matrices that would need to be calculated and then used for calculations in each and every RRPP iteration.  We use a lot of stratagems to save computer memory and reduce the redundant calculations of large matrices, but I have not yet been able to conjure computational miracles (I’m trying!).  The best I could do in your shoes is turn to a computer I have in the lab with 32 threaded cores and several hundred gigabytes of RAM, start an analysis, and maybe come back in one day to one week to see if I have results.  I would not attempt such a thing on my MacBook.

If one is savvy enough, they could do their own parametric analyses to eliminate RRPP, and maybe run bilat.symmetry with just 1 iteration to get the non-statistical portions of the analysis (like symmetric and asymmetric shape components).  As a lark, I decided to think about how long that could be expected to take.  You did not provide information for the number and type of landmarks used, so let’s just do something simple like 15 2D landmarks (30 Procrustes residuals).  I make up some data and do the following:

> Y <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(X) * 30), nrow(X), 30)
> system.time(fit <- lm(Y ~ ind/side))
   user  system elapsed 
386.022   6.287 401.052 

So it takes nearly 7 minutes just to fit a linear model on my computer.  (With RRPP fitting this model plus at least two others for shape, plus the same number for size, times say 1000 iterations… I won’t do the math but you can see it is a very long time.)  Performing a parametric MANOVA is also not an easy chore

> system.time(fitM <- manova(fit))
   user  system elapsed 
384.381   2.271 387.217 

And to do such an analysis assumes you have few shape variables compared to the number of observations, which I hope with 18,000 observations is a safe assumption.

Thus, I think we can abate your concerns that the function is working properly and confirm your conclusion that the analysis is taking forever is probably perceptively accurate. My advice is to do one of the following:

1. Consider performing bilateral symmetry analyses separately on subsets of data, maybe four analyses, one each for each location.  This might still be painfully long but more manageable.

2. Perform the analysis on a small portion of the data to make sure it works properly and then schedule some time at a facility with a super computer to run a whole analysis, taking advantage of parallel processing capabilities.

3. “Hard-wire” an analysis of appropriate linear models using parametric MANOVA instead of RRPP.  The non-statistical portions of bilat.symmetry (e.g., symmetric shape component, asymmetric shape component) can still be obtained by running an analysis with iter = 0.  It will still take a long time, but it will only seem like forever.

But regardless of choice, you must accept the fact — as I am sure you have! — that you have a huge data set and quick results simply are not likely.  

Good luck!
Mike
